title: Algor mortis
prompt: After death, a clothed adult in a room around 70 °F cools by roughly how much per hour?
explain: A common teaching rule is about 1.5 °F (0.8 °C) per hour, often after a short plateau. It's a rough guide: room temperature, clothing, body size, air flow and wet clothing all change the rate, which is why real estimates use corrected methods and give wide ranges.

sources.cite: Henssge C, Madea B. Estimation of the time since death in the early post-mortem period. Forensic Science International. 2004;144(2-3):167-175.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Algor mortis
prompt: A body measures 92.6 °F in a 70 °F room. Using the 1.5 °F per hour rule, roughly how long since death?
explain: 98.6 − 92.6 = 6 °F lost, and 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 hours. Treat it as a centre point with an hour or two either side, not an exact answer.

sources.cite: Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Rigor mortis
prompt: Rigor mortis usually becomes noticeable first in which muscles?
options: Small muscles such as the jaw
All muscles at the same moment
explain: Stiffening is usually noticed first in small muscles (jaw, face, neck) a few hours after death, spreads to the arms and then the legs, is typically complete by around 12 hours, and passes off over the following day or two. Heat speeds it up and cold slows it down.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Rigor mortis
prompt: The jaw and arms are stiff, but the legs still move freely. What does that suggest?
explain: Rigor that has reached the arms but not yet the legs is still developing, which typically means a few hours to most of a working day. Fully stiff joints suggest about 8 hours or more; loosening again suggests a day or more.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.

title: Livor mortis
prompt: Pooled blood (livor) that still blanches when you press it with a thumb usually means…
options: It hasn't fixed yet: usually under about 8–12 hours
Death was more than two days ago
explain: After circulation stops, blood settles by gravity into the lowest parts of the body and becomes visible within about half an hour to a few hours. It blanches under pressure at first and becomes fixed, no longer blanching, at very roughly 8–12 hours.

sources.cite: Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.
National Institute of Justice. Death Investigation: A Guide for the Scene Investigator. Technical update, 2011.

title: Livor mortis
prompt: A person is found face up, but fixed livor is on the front of the body. What should an investigator suspect?
options: The body was moved after the livor fixed
explain: Livor forms on whatever side was lowest. Fixed livor that doesn't match the position the body was found in means the body was moved some hours after death, which is always worth explaining.

sources.cite: National Institute of Justice. Death Investigation: A Guide for the Scene Investigator. Technical update, 2011.

title: Gastric contents
prompt: How reliable is the state of the stomach for timing a death?
options: Precise to within half an hour
Rough at best: emptying varies widely
explain: A meal often leaves the stomach within roughly 2–6 hours, but meal size, fat content, stress, illness and drugs change that a lot. Stomach contents can support other evidence, especially when the meal time is known, but never replace it.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Gastric contents
prompt: Dinner was at 7 PM and the stomach is still full of barely digested food. Death was most likely…
options: Within a couple of hours of dinner
explain: A full stomach of barely digested food suggests death came fairly soon after the meal, within a couple of hours or so. It's a supporting clue, not proof: emptying can stall in some illnesses and stressful situations.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.

title: Scene conditions
prompt: The window was open on a cold night. Compared with the 1.5 °F per hour rule, the body probably cooled…
options: Faster, so death was more recent than the rule suggests
explain: Colder surroundings speed cooling, so the same temperature drop took less time. A warm room does the opposite. Record the scene's conditions, including room temperature, before anything changes, and adjust or widen the estimate.

sources.cite: National Institute of Justice. Death Investigation: A Guide for the Scene Investigator. Technical update, 2011.
Henssge C, Madea B. Estimation of the time since death in the early post-mortem period. Forensic Science International. 2004;144(2-3):167-175.

title: Scene conditions
prompt: Why should the room temperature be measured as soon as investigators arrive?
options: Opening doors and windows changes it, and the cooling estimate depends on it
It shows the cause of death
explain: Every body-temperature estimate depends on the surrounding temperature. Once people come and go, doors and windows open and heating changes, so the conditions the body actually cooled in are lost unless they're recorded first.

sources.cite: National Institute of Justice. Death Investigation: A Guide for the Scene Investigator. Technical update, 2011.

title: Coronary disease
prompt: A 90% narrowing of a main coronary artery can cause sudden death mainly by…
explain: Severe narrowing starves the heart muscle of oxygen, especially under strain, and an oxygen-starved heart can fall into a fatal rhythm (an arrhythmia) within minutes. Often the only warning is tiredness, breathlessness or indigestion.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Coronary disease
prompt: In a sudden cardiac death, why are the lungs often heavy with fluid?
options: The failing heart couldn't pump, so fluid backed up into the lungs
explain: When the left side of the heart fails, pressure builds up in the vessels of the lungs and fluid seeps into them (pulmonary edema). It supports a cardiac death but isn't specific to it.

sources.cite: Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Manner of death
prompt: Which of these is a manner of death?
explain: A death certificate separates the cause (the disease or injury that started it, like coronary artery disease), the mechanism (what physically happened, like a fatal rhythm) and the manner: one of natural, accident, suicide, homicide or undetermined, with 'pending' while tests are out.

sources.cite: National Center for Health Statistics. Medical Examiners' and Coroners' Handbook on Death Registration and Fetal Death Reporting. CDC; 2003.
Hanzlick R, Hunsaker JC, Davis GJ. A Guide for Manner of Death Classification. National Association of Medical Examiners; 2002.

title: Manner of death
prompt: On a death certificate, a manner of 'homicide' means…
options: Death at the hands of another person; not a legal finding of murder
A court has found someone guilty
explain: Homicide as a manner of death is a medical classification: death resulting from another person's actions. Whether it was a crime, and whose, is for the police and courts to decide.

sources.cite: Hanzlick R, Hunsaker JC, Davis GJ. A Guide for Manner of Death Classification. National Association of Medical Examiners; 2002.
National Center for Health Statistics. Medical Examiners' and Coroners' Handbook on Death Registration and Fetal Death Reporting. CDC; 2003.

title: Toxicology levels
prompt: A drug found at a 'therapeutic' level in postmortem blood usually means…
options: It was taken as prescribed, and isn't by itself a cause of death
The person died of an overdose
explain: Reference books list the blood levels seen with normal use, with toxic and fatal ranges. A therapeutic level fits normal use, though it can still matter: a normal dose of a blood thinner can worsen a bleed.

sources.cite: Baselt RC. Disposition of Toxic Drugs and Chemicals in Man. Biomedical Publications (current edition).

title: Toxicology levels
prompt: Why can a drug's level in blood taken after death be higher than it was at the moment of death?
options: Drugs keep being made by the body
Drugs can move out of organs into the blood after death
explain: This is postmortem redistribution: some drugs stored in organs such as the lungs and liver leak back into nearby blood after death. That's why samples are usually taken from a leg vein rather than the heart.

sources.cite: Pélissier-Alicot AL, Gaulier JM, Champsaur P, Marquet P. Mechanisms underlying postmortem redistribution of drugs: a review. Journal of Analytical Toxicology. 2003;27(8):533-544.
Baselt RC. Disposition of Toxic Drugs and Chemicals in Man. Biomedical Publications (current edition).

title: Blood thinners
prompt: Why does a blood thinner such as warfarin matter when an older person falls?
options: It slows clotting, so a minor head injury can cause a large bleed
It causes dizziness that always leads to falls
explain: Anticoagulants reduce the blood's ability to clot. After a blow to the head, a bleed that would stop on its own can keep growing. Many deaths after minor falls in older people involve these medicines.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Blood thinners
prompt: Someone on warfarin falls, hits their head and dies of the bleed. What is the manner of death?
options: Accident: the fall caused the injury; the medicine made it worse
explain: The manner follows what started the chain of events. An injury from a fall is an accident, even if a prescribed medicine made the injury deadlier.

sources.cite: Hanzlick R, Hunsaker JC, Davis GJ. A Guide for Manner of Death Classification. National Association of Medical Examiners; 2002.

title: Head injury
prompt: Bruising of the brain on the side OPPOSITE the point of impact (contrecoup) usually means…
options: A moving head struck a fixed surface, as in a fall
explain: When a moving head stops suddenly against the floor, the brain keeps moving and bruises against the opposite side of the skull. A blow to a still head usually injures the brain under the impact (coup) without a contrecoup bruise.

sources.cite: Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.
DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.

title: Head injury
prompt: Injuries above the 'hat brim line' of the head are more typical of…
explain: Falls from standing tend to injure the head at or below the line where a hat brim would sit. Injuries above it, especially several of them, are more typical of blows. It's a guide, not proof: falls down stairs can break the rule.

sources.cite: Kremer C, Racette S, Dionne CA, Sauvageau A. Discrimination of falls and blows in blunt head trauma: systematic study of the hat brim line rule in relation to skull fractures. Journal of Forensic Sciences. 2008;53(3):716-719.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.

title: Blunt force
prompt: Bruises on the backs of the forearms in an assault are often called…
explain: Raising the arms to ward off blows puts the backs of the forearms and hands in the way. Their absence doesn't prove there was no assault, but their presence is a strong clue.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.

title: Blunt force
prompt: How does a laceration differ from a cut (an incised wound)?
options: A laceration is a tear from blunt force, with ragged edges and strands of tissue bridging it
explain: Blunt force crushes and splits the skin, leaving bruised, irregular edges with bridges of tissue across the gap. A sharp edge cuts cleanly through everything, leaving no bridges.

sources.cite: DiMaio VJ, DiMaio D. Forensic Pathology. 2nd ed. CRC Press; 2001.
Saukko P, Knight B. Knight's Forensic Pathology. 4th ed. CRC Press; 2016.
